lines.en: Tessa, **did you hear about** the new bridge downtown?
lines.pt: Tessa, você ficou sabendo da nova ponte no centro?

lines.en: **Apparently,** it opens this Saturday, after three years of work.
lines.pt: Pelo visto, ela abre neste sábado, depois de três anos de obras.

lines.en: Wow. **I read that** there will be a street festival, too.
lines.pt: Uau. Li que também vai ter um festival de rua.

lines.en: Is that right? Where did you read it?
On the city’s website. But **I’m not sure** about the time.

lines.en: Let me check. **According to** the mayor’s office, it starts at ten a.m.

pages.title: Cultural snapshot — Sharing news
pages.intro: How you share news says as much as the news itself. Look and guess before you read.

cards.note: A friendly opening for news or gossip, often followed by the details.
“I read that…” and “According to…” show where the information comes from.
“Apparently” and “I’m not sure” warn that you have not confirmed it.

levels.A2: To say they heard it, but are not 100% sure.
levels.B1: It signals that the information comes from someone else and may need checking.
levels.B2: It distances the speaker from the claim, hedging responsibility for its accuracy.

qs.q: Why name the source of news?

levels.A2: So people know where it comes from.
levels.B1: It helps listeners trust or check the information.
levels.B2: Attribution lets listeners judge reliability and protects you from spreading unverified claims.

qs.q: How can you react to news?

levels.B1: Is that right? That’s interesting. I hadn’t heard that.
levels.B2: Short reactions like “Is that right?” or “Wow, I had no idea” invite the speaker to add details.

pages.compare: In Brazil, “fiquei sabendo que…” and “dizem que…” do a similar job of hedging. In English, “Apparently…” and “I read that…” are the usual tools. Which ones do you use?

teach.goal: Entender como se compartilham notícias com cuidado: fonte e grau de certeza.
solo: Mostre os 3 cartões e peça hipóteses.

extra: Have you ever shared a rumor that was false?

stretch: B2: discuta por que citar a fonte importa na era das redes sociais.

pages.title: Level up — the same situation from A1 to C2
pages.intro: The situation stays the same; the language grows in length, nuance and autonomy.

ladder.goal: Share news with a few key words.

ladder.say: Did you hear about the bridge? It opens on Saturday.
ladder.goal: Share news with a simple opening.

ladder.say: Apparently, the bridge opens on Saturday, but I’m not sure about the time.
ladder.goal: Share news with a source and hedge.

ladder.say: According to the city, the bridge is due to open on Saturday, although there has been no official confirmation of the time.
ladder.goal: Report news with attribution and precision.

ladder.say: While the city insists the bridge will open on Saturday, I’d take that with a pinch of salt given the delays so far.
One suspects the Saturday date is aspirational at best, given how long that bridge has taken.
ladder.goal: Comment on news with tone and irony.

pages.note: This progression is illustrative: complex sentences do not define a level on their own. CEFR also considers comprehension, autonomy, fluency, accuracy, interaction and appropriateness.
